subject: Polity
sub_topic: Legislative relations — Union, State, Concurrent lists

concepts.name: Structure and Composition of the Three Lists (Seventh Schedule)
key_dimensions: Exact number of entries in each list (Union: 100, State: 61, Concurrent: 52) and common UPSC traps on miscounting
Original vs. current entry counts after 42nd Amendment reshuffling (education, forests, weights & measures moved to Concurrent)
Nature of entries as 'fields of legislation' not exhaustive grants — residuary power implication
Which list has NO residuary power and how that differs from the Canadian model

concepts.name: Residuary Powers of Parliament (Article 248 & Entry 97, Union List)
key_dimensions: Constitutional basis: Article 248 read with Entry 97 of Union List — Parliament's exclusive power over residuary subjects
Contrast with USA (residuary with states) and Canada (residuary with Centre) — India closer to Canada
Judicial test for identifying 'residuary' subject: whether it falls in any existing entry after liberal construction
Levy of GST on goods and services as a contemporary residuary/constitutional amendment example

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation on State List: Article 249 (National Interest)
key_dimensions: Procedural trigger: Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3rd majority of members present and voting (not total membership)
Temporal limit: Resolution valid for 1 year, renewable; law ceases to operate 6 months after resolution lapses
Scope: Only during resolution period; states are NOT suspended — they can legislate simultaneously
UPSC trap: Article 249 does NOT require a national emergency; it is a peacetime provision distinct from Article 250

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation on State List During National Emergency: Article 250
key_dimensions: Operative condition: Proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 must be in force
Parliament acquires power to legislate on ANY entry in the State List — not just specific ones
Sunset clause: Law made under Article 250 ceases to operate 6 months after emergency ceases
Contrast with Article 249: No Rajya Sabha resolution needed; President's proclamation itself is the trigger
Coexistence with state laws: Parliamentary law prevails during emergency; state law revives after

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation on State List: Article 252 (Two or More States Consent)
key_dimensions: Mechanism: Two or more state legislatures pass resolutions requesting Parliament to legislate on a State List subject
Binding nature: Only consenting states are bound; other states can adopt the law by passing similar resolution
Irrevocability trap: Once Parliament legislates under Article 252, the consenting state CANNOT repeal or amend it
Real examples: Prize Competition Act 1955, Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974
Distinction from Article 253: Article 252 is state-initiated; Article 253 is treaty/international agreement-initiated

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation on State List: Article 253 (International Treaties)
key_dimensions: Scope: Parliament can legislate on any subject (including State List) to implement international treaties, agreements, or conventions
No state consent required — a significant centralising provision
Judicial interpretation: Must have a 'real and substantial' connection to the international obligation (BALCO case angle)
Contemporary relevance: Climate change conventions, WTO obligations, TRIPS — can override state powers
Contrast with Article 252: Article 253 is Union-initiated and unilateral; not limited to consenting states

concepts.name: Repugnancy Doctrine: Article 254 and Centre-State Concurrent List Conflict
key_dimensions: Core rule: In case of repugnancy between Central and State law on Concurrent List, Central law prevails and State law is void to the extent of repugnancy
Exception (Article 254(2)): State law can prevail IF it has received Presidential assent — but Parliament can still override later
Judicial test for 'repugnancy': Direct conflict test AND occupied field test (M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India)
UPSC trap: Repugnancy rule applies ONLY to Concurrent List — not when Centre legislates on State List under special provisions
State law under 254(2) does not become Central law — it remains state law with temporary override ability

concepts.name: Presidential Assent to State Bills: Articles 200 and 201
key_dimensions: Four options for Governor: Assent, Withhold, Return for reconsideration, Reserve for President's consideration
Mandatory reservation cases: Bills affecting High Court powers (Article 200), Bills on Concurrent List conflicting with Central law
President's options under Article 201: Assent, Withhold, or direct Governor to return — President has NO obligation to assent
Pocket veto issue: No time limit prescribed for President to act on reserved bills — recent controversies (Kerala, Punjab governors)
SC ruling in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary (2023): Governor cannot indefinitely withhold assent — constitutional convention matters

concepts.name: Doctrine of Pith and Substance in Legislative Entries
key_dimensions: Core principle: A law is valid if its 'true nature and character' (pith and substance) falls within the legislating body's competence, even if it incidentally trenches on another list
Origin: Privy Council in Cushing v. Dupuy; applied in India in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
Distinguishing from 'colourable legislation': Pith and substance tests bona fide purpose; colourable legislation tests disguised encroachment
Application: Used to resolve Union List vs. State List conflicts more than Concurrent List conflicts
Limitation: Cannot be used to justify legislation that is substantially on a subject outside competence

concepts.name: Doctrine of Colourable Legislation
key_dimensions: Maxim: 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' — legislature cannot do indirectly what it has no power to do directly
Key case: K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa — Orissa Estates Abolition Act challenged
Relationship with pith and substance: Both deal with legislative competence but colourable legislation focuses on mala fide/disguised intent
Application in taxation: States cannot impose what is essentially a Union tax by labelling it differently
UPSC trap: Colourable legislation doctrine applies to legislative competence, NOT to violation of fundamental rights

concepts.name: Entries in Lists: Rule of Liberal and Harmonious Construction
key_dimensions: Principle: Entries in all three lists must be given widest possible meaning; narrow/pedantic interpretation avoided
Harmonious construction rule: If an act can be brought under two entries, courts prefer the interpretation that makes it valid
GVK Industries v. Union of India: Supreme Court held entries should be construed to avoid overlap and constitutional conflict
Specific list hierarchy: In case of genuine overlap, Union List > Concurrent List > State List
Comparison with American dual federalism: India uses cooperative/pragmatic construction rather than strict separation

concepts.name: 42nd Amendment (1976): Redistribution of Legislative Entries
key_dimensions: Subjects transferred from State List to Concurrent List: Education (Entry 25), Forests (Entry 17A), Protection of wild animals (Entry 17B), Weights and Measures, Administration of justice
Significance: Significant centralisation during Emergency — reduced state autonomy in key social sectors
Post-42nd Amendment effect on education: Centre can now set national education policy framework (NEP 2020 constitutional basis)
Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission recommendations: Restore some subjects to State List to strengthen federalism
UPSC trap: 'Education' is now in Concurrent List (Entry 25), NOT State List — common confusion source

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation on State List During President's Rule: Article 356 Read with Article 357
key_dimensions: Article 357(1): During President's Rule, Parliament can confer on President power to legislate on State List OR delegate this to any authority
Article 357(2): Laws made by Parliament/President during President's Rule continue to operate AFTER President's Rule ends unless repealed by state
Key distinction from Article 250: Laws under Article 357 survive after emergency; laws under Article 250 lapse 6 months after emergency
S.R. Bommai case relevance: Imposition of President's Rule itself scrutinised — legislative power flows only from valid proclamation
UPSC trap: Parliament can delegate legislative power under Article 357 — an exception to the general non-delegation doctrine

concepts.name: Inter-State Water Disputes and Legislative Competence (Entry 17, 56 — Union/State Lists)
key_dimensions: Entry 17, State List: Water (water supplies, irrigation, canals, drainage) — ordinarily a state subject
Entry 56, Union List: Regulation and development of inter-State rivers — Parliament can legislate if declared expedient in public interest
Article 262: Parliament may exclude Supreme Court jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes — UNIQUE exclusion of judicial review
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956 and Tribunal mechanism — recent amendment (2019) for permanent tribunal
UPSC trap: Article 262 is one of very few provisions that can exclude Supreme Court's jurisdiction — often tested

concepts.name: Taxation Entries and the Union-State Division (No Concurrent List for Taxes)
key_dimensions: Critical principle: There are NO taxation entries in the Concurrent List — taxes are exclusively either Union or State
Article 246A (101st Amendment, GST): Simultaneous power to levy GST — a de facto 'concurrent' taxation power created by constitutional amendment
Distinction between 'fee' and 'tax': Fee for service can be levied by states even on Union List subjects (Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. case)
Entry 92C (Union List) — taxes on services: Inserted by 88th Amendment but never brought into force; subsumed by GST
UPSC trap: GST under Article 246A is NOT placed in any list — it is a special provision outside the three-list scheme

concepts.name: GST and Article 246A: Concurrent Taxing Power and Federal Restructuring
key_dimensions: Article 246A (inserted by 101st Amendment 2016): Both Parliament and State Legislatures have power to make laws on GST
Exception within Article 246A: Parliament ALONE has power over inter-state supply of goods and services (IGST)
GST Council (Article 279A): A new constitutional federal body — recommendations not binding but carry persuasive authority (SC in Union v. Mohit Minerals 2022)
Impact on legislative lists: Several entries in Union and State lists amended/deleted (e.g., Entry 84 Union List, Entry 54 State List modified)
Federal bargain: States gave up exclusive tax powers in exchange for compensation mechanism — cooperative federalism model

concepts.name: Doctrine of Occupied Field in Concurrent List Legislation
key_dimensions: Concept: Even without direct conflict, if Parliament has 'occupied the field' comprehensively, state cannot legislate on the same subject
Distinction from direct repugnancy: Occupied field = Parliament's intent to cover the whole area; direct conflict = contradictory provisions
Key case: Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay — Central law occupied the field of essential commodities
State can still legislate in gaps deliberately left by Parliament — intentional lacuna vs. occupied field
UPSC trap: 'Occupied field' can void a state law even if the state law is NOT contradictory to Central law — this is counter-intuitive

concepts.name: Special Provisions for Certain States and Legislative Relations (Articles 371-371J)
key_dimensions: Article 371A (Nagaland): No Parliamentary law on Nagaland's customary law and practices without State Assembly's resolution — UNIQUE protection
Article 371G (Mizoram): Similar protection for Mizo customary law — Parliament cannot override without state assembly resolution
Significance: Creates asymmetric federalism — these states have veto over Central legislation on specific subjects
Contrast with general rule: Normally states cannot block Parliamentary legislation; Articles 371A/371G are explicit exceptions
UPSC trap: These protections are NOT in the regular three lists — they are special constitutional provisions overriding normal legislative relations

concepts.name: Centre's Power to Give Directions to States on Legislative/Executive Matters: Articles 256-257
key_dimensions: Article 256: States must ensure laws made by Parliament are complied with — executive power of state must not impede Parliament's laws
Article 257: Centre can give directions to states for protection of railways, maintenance of means of communication declared to be of national/military importance
Article 257A (deleted by 44th Amendment): Was inserted by 42nd Amendment — allowed deployment of armed forces in states without consent
Consequence of non-compliance: Failure to comply with Union directions can be a ground for President's Rule under Article 356
UPSC trap: Article 257A was DELETED — if asked about Centre's power to deploy armed forces in states, this provision no longer exists

concepts.name: Sarkaria and Punchhi Commission Recommendations on Legislative Relations
key_dimensions: Sarkaria Commission (1983): Recommended restoring subjects from Concurrent to State List; Article 249 should be used sparingly; prior consultation with states before concurrent legislation
Punchhi Commission (2007): Recommended codifying Centre's obligation to consult states on Concurrent List legislation; suggested 'localisation' principle for Concurrent List
Inter-State Council (Article 263): Recommended as primary forum for Centre-State legislative coordination — underutilised
Critical gap: Neither commission recommendations are legally binding — implementation depends on political will
UPSC angle: Commissions' recommendations are frequently tested as 'measures to strengthen federalism' in Mains answers
